\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our consensus-proximity selection is equivalent to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling} with Set Jaccard as the utility function: $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
MBR decoding has shown strong results in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high}, where output diversity is high and utility functions (e.g., BLEURT) correlate well with human quality judgments.
In structured IE, however, constrained decoding compresses per-sample diversity, and set-level overlap is a weaker proxy for extraction quality than trained MT metrics---explaining why MBR-style selection fails here despite its success in translation.
tool_args.new_string:
\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling} with different utility functions: SJ selection uses $U{=}\text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, EM selection uses $U{=}\mathbb{1}[y_i{=}y_j]$ (equivalent to standard self-consistency majority voting), and Voting selection uses entity-level majority overlap.
Each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$---a direct MBR instantiation.
MBR has theoretical optimality guarantees when the utility function aligns with the true evaluation metric \cite{eikema2022sampling}, and strong empirical results in machine translation where learned utilities (e.g., BLEURT) correlate well with human judgments \cite{freitag2022high}.

That we tested five distinct MBR variants---each with a different utility function---and \textit{all} failed to surpass greedy strengthens rather than weakens our negative result.
The failure cannot be attributed to a poor choice of utility; it reflects systematic utility-quality misalignment at the per-sample level.
Our quality estimation results show that these same utility functions \textit{do} correlate with F1 at the instance level (AUROC up to 0.75): averaging $U(y_i, y_j)$ over all $j$ produces scores that distinguish easy from hard instances.
But MBR selection requires a stronger property---that $U(y_i, y_j)$ discriminates among candidates \textit{within} a single instance---and this is precisely where alignment breaks down.
This per-sample utility-quality misalignment is the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Test-time scaling through multi-sample generation promises quality improvements for LLM-based information extraction, but which confidence signals best serve quality estimation versus sample selection remains unclear.
3	We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting, Soft Jaccard), surface (exact match, Fleiss' $\kappa$), and model-internal (log-probability)---across NER (three datasets of varying difficulty) and RE (SciERC) with two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B).
4	We find that the strongest signals achieve $\rho{=}0.38$ (entity voting) and AUROC${=}0.75$ (exact match) for quality estimation, with ranking and classification favoring different signals across task complexity; however, this strong quality estimation does not translate into selection gains---we find no statistically significant evidence that any signal surpasses greedy decoding in any of six tested configurations spanning two models and three datasets ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
5	We term this disconnect the \textit{correlation-selection gap}: instance-level consistency signals predict which inputs the model handles reliably, not which output is best among $N$ candidates.
6	Signal rankings further depend on task difficulty---exact match dominates easy tasks, structural signals dominate hard tasks, and when model capability is insufficient, apparent correlations are driven by zero/non-zero separation rather than genuine quality gradation---establishing that signal choice should be guided by task difficulty and intended application.
7	These results reframe consistency signals as quality estimators rather than output selectors for structured IE.
8	\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
4	On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
5	More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2024scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
6	These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
7	For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
8	But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
9	The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
10	There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
11	Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?
